summary:
The Sun is the rover's lifeline: without enough sunlight, its battery drains, leaving it stranded and blind. Earth is its link to mission control: lose that connection, and our voice falls silent in the depths of space.

We built a suite of tools to help mission teams see those risks before choosing where to land or travel:

The ranked site board compares candidate locations by sunlight, Earth visibility and rover power, so teams can find the sites that best support the rover's energy and communication needs.
The interactive terrain map shows slopes, craters, shadows and places where terrain may block sunlight or communication, so teams can spot hazards before they become obstacles.
The time scrubber follows the Sun and Earth across the lunar sky and shows how battery and communication change, so teams can see when the rover may lose power or contact.
Forecast overlays show where sunlight or Earth visibility will improve or get worse in the hours ahead, giving teams time to plan around changing conditions.
3D orbit and surface views bring selected south pole sites into closer focus, so teams understand the landscape before committing to a landing or route.
Together, these tools help teams anticipate hazards, protect the rover and reduce the risk of it being stranded or cut off from mission control, making our odyssey among the stars a little less perilous.
details:
What it does and how it works
The Lunar Landing Site Navigator shows when the Sun (power) and Earth (direct-to-Earth comms) rise above the real terrain horizon at any point on the Moon. It turns that into rover survival numbers and compares sites side by side.

  1. Ephemeris. We compute Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation from any lunar latitude and longitude with NASA NAIF SPICE (spiceypy). The kernels are DE440 planetary ephemeris, the high-precision lunar orientation file moon_pa_de440 (so libration is included), the Moon frame kernel and leap-second kernels. Everything runs offline at any time step.
  2. Terrain horizon. We load LOLA elevation models from the NASA PDS with rasterio and numpy:
  • LDEM_85S_20M, the 20 m south polar map, cropped to 45 km around the south pole sites
  • LDEM_64, the global map, for everywhere else and for the far horizon

For each site we ray-march along great circles in 720 directions (every 0.5°). Steps are 20 m out to 12 km and 160 m from there to 150 km. We apply the drop from lunar curvature and put the observer on a 2 m mast. The highest elevation angle in each direction gives a 360° skyline.

  1. Model.
  • Sun disc: we treat the Sun as a disc, not a point. The fraction above the skyline is f = 1 − (acos x − x√(1−x²))/π, where x = (sun_el − skyline_el)/0.267°.
  • Eclipses: solar eclipses (Earth crossing the Sun) are modelled as the overlap of the two discs, sized from SPICE distances, and reduce f further.
  • Power: P = 1361 · area · efficiency · cos(sun_el) · f.
  • Battery: charge is integrated as charge += (P − load)·dt and kept between 0 and full capacity.
  • Comms margin: Earth elevation minus the skyline in Earth's direction. Below 0° the link is blocked, 0° to 0.5° is marginal, and above 0.5° it is clear.
  • Outputs: % of time sunlit, Wh/day, longest night, minimum battery, survives yes/no, % of time Earth is visible, longest blackout, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, and % of time with both power and comms.
  1. Rover defaults. The rover numbers come from NASA's VIPER rover (NASA NTRS 20240013903; NASA Science, VIPER In Depth):
  • 5,420 Wh battery
  • 108 W low-power load (battery capacity divided by NASA's 50-hour survival figure)
  • 1.1 m² of panel at 30% efficiency, which matches VIPER's 450 W peak

Users can pick the VIPER preset or enter their own solar power, battery capacity and load.

  1. Site presets. Every preset cites its source:
  • Malapert Massif: NASA's notional Artemis III site (Kring et al. 2025). It is on NASA's October 2024 list of nine Artemis III regions.
  • Peak near Shackleton: the highest point of NASA's LOLA 5 m "Site07" terrain (NASA PGDA; Barker et al. 2021), 0.7 km from the persistently lit spot given in Mahanti et al. 2024.
  • Connecting Ridge: the crest of NASA's LOLA 5 m "Site01" terrain (NASA PGDA; Barker et al. 2021; numbering after Mazarico et al. 2011).
  • Shackleton crater floor: the crater centre from the IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, kept as the permanently dark case.
  • Apollo 11 and 17: the lunar module positions from NASA NSSDC.
  1. Per-cell visibility maps. The backend sends a 241 × 241 height grid at 100 m around the site (about 96 kB gzipped). For every cell, the browser computes the share of the Sun's disc that cell sees and whether it has a clear line to Earth, by sweeping toward each body over the curved surface. A Web Worker computes forecast frames ahead of the time cursor and caches them, keeping the last 40. It then draws a heatmap of where conditions will get better or worse over the coming hours. While the user drags the cursor, a quick 200 m version is shown first and replaced with the full-detail version once it is ready.
  2. Interface.
  • A ranked site board.
  • A 360° skyline panorama with the Sun and Earth tracks.
  • Charts of power, battery and comms over time.
  • A time scrubber that plays a full year of time steps smoothly.
  • A shaded 2D terrain map with the forecast overlays.
  • A 3D Unity WebGL view built on NASA's LOLA 5 m terrain (NASA PGDA). In the sky, Earth is drawn as a globe with NASA's Blue Marble texture, lit from the Sun's direction so its phase is correct. At the site stands a full-size rover: NASA's Perseverance 3D model, used in place of VIPER because NASA has not published a VIPER model.
  • Compare mode for up to 4 sites, with the best value for each metric highlighted.

Benefits
The tool answers "will a rover survive here, and can it phone home?" with numbers, not just pictures of lighting. Pairing the terrain horizon with a battery simulation exposes the failure that matters most: the longest night, when the battery runs out. The forecast overlays show conditions changing hour by hour across the area around a site, not only at one point.

Intended impact
Mission planners, students and the public can check Artemis-era south pole sites in seconds and in a browser, with no GIS or SPICE expertise. For example, our model gives Peak near Shackleton 87.9% sunlight over 2027 with a longest night of 248 h. Malapert Massif gets 71.0% sunlight but keeps Earth in view 100% of the time. The trade-off between power and comms becomes visible at a glance.

Tools, languages and software

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, NumPy, SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE), rasterio, pytest, HTTPX, Docker.
    • NASA NAIF SPICE kernels
    • NASA PDS LOLA elevation models
    • NASA PGDA LOLA 5 m south pole terrain
    • NASA Blue Marble imagery
    • NASA Perseverance 3D model
    • NASA NSSDC Apollo coordinates
    • NASA's Artemis III region list
    • VIPER specifications (NASA NTRS, NASA Science)
    • IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature
    • peer-reviewed papers: Kring et al. 2025, Mahanti et al. 2024, Barker et al. 2021, Mazarico et al. 2011
  • Development: Claude Code (AI coding assistant).

How it is creative

  • It follows a mission question from the sky through the horizon and power to whether the rover survives, rather than stopping at illumination maps.
  • The forecast overlay shows where light and Earth visibility will get better or worse in the hours ahead, computed per cell in the browser.
  • A dot-matrix "mission board" interface shows lit, dark and blocked states the way a control-room panel would.
  • Eclipses are part of the model: a solar eclipse seen from the Moon shows up as a dip in the battery.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy over approximation:
    • real ephemeris with libration, not simplified orbits
    • the Sun treated as a disc, so a half-risen Sun gives partial power
    • lunar curvature included out to 150 km
    • a 2 m mast height
    • eclipse occultation
    • two map resolutions keep memory small
    • the per-cell grid is gzipped
    • forecast work runs in a background worker
    • a quick preview shows while scrubbing
